metadata.title: School efficiency in low and middle income countries: An analysis based on PISA for development learning survey

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the 2017 PISA for Development (PISA-D) microdata merged across student, teacher, and school/principal questionnaires, but the paper does not report applying any PISA-D sampling or student weights in the DEA and second-stage regressions. The analytic sample is defined at the school level (1180 schools) after excluding missing values on DEA inputs, and all DEA inputs/outputs are computed as school-level averages. Because the methodology is Data Envelopment Analysis with bootstrap bias correction (1000 repetitions for DEA scores and 2000 for second-stage coefficients), the paper’s uncertainty quantification comes from bootstrap resampling rather than from replicate-weight variance estimation. Analysts using the OECD/PISA-D database should still consider the original complex survey design when interpreting generalizability, but the manuscript provides no explicit weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedure.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses merged 2017 PISA-D data (students, teachers, and schools/principals) for seven LMIC/economies at grade 7 (15-year-olds) or above. The paper reports a total PISA-D sample of 34,604 students, 15,169 teachers, and 1,299 schools, but the DEA analysis is conducted at the school level. The final working sample contains 1180 schools after excluding missing values on DEA inputs. All DEA inputs and outputs are computed as school-level averages; cognitive outputs use math/reading/science scores derived from plausible values, while non-cognitive outputs use factor-analysis-derived indices (socialisation, attitudes, feelings).

confounders_identified.variable_name: Repeat if does not achieve minimum standard
No test language at home share

main_findings.target_variable: Cognitive technical efficiency (DEA output-oriented, VRS; bias-corrected TEBC)
top_predictors: Does not speak test language at home share
main_findings.performance_metrics: Mean TEBC (cognitive): 0.801 (SD 0.083); country TEBC range: 0.761 (Zambia) to 0.861 (Ecuador). Bootstrap performance: 26.217; 95% CI for whole-sample TEBC: [0.770, 0.833]. Second-stage marginal effects (M2, cognitive): e.g., Repeat (lower secondary) −0.0863 (SE 0.0150, p<0.05), Work −0.0609 (SE 0.0111, p<0.01), Home language not test language −0.0543 (SE 0.0086, p<0.01), Preschool attended +0.0233 (SE 0.0100, p<0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA-D 2017 Grade 7+ the study estimated cognitive technical efficiency at the school level using DEA with cognitive outputs derived from the first plausible value for math/reading/science, and then related the bias-corrected efficiency scores to student, teacher, and school characteristics. It found that the average cognitive TEBC was 0.801, implying scope to increase cognitive outputs by about 20% while holding inputs constant, and that disadvantaged student conditions (repetition, work, and not speaking the test language at home) significantly reduced cognitive efficiency. This indicates that policies targeting attendance barriers and language disadvantages—alongside early support such as preschool attendance—may improve school performance efficiency in LMIC, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

main_findings.target_variable: Non-cognitive technical efficiency (DEA output-oriented, VRS; bias-corrected TEBC)
top_predictors: Does not speak test language at home share
main_findings.performance_metrics: Mean TEBC (non-cognitive): 0.782 (SD 0.078); country TEBC range: 0.737 (Zambia) to 0.802 (Ecuador). Bootstrap performance: 26.632; 95% CI for whole-sample TEBC: [0.749, 0.813]. Second-stage marginal effects (M2, non-cognitive): e.g., Work −0.0609 (SE 0.0111, p<0.01), Skipped whole day −0.0615 (SE 0.0074, p<0.01), Home language not test language −0.0214 (SE 0.0087, p<0.05), Classroom climate index +0.0413 (SE 0.0053, p<0.01), School expectations −0.0492 (SE 0.0054, p<0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA-D 2017 Grade 7+ the study estimated non-cognitive technical efficiency at the school level using DEA with non-cognitive outputs (socialisation, attitudes, feelings) and then modeled bias-corrected efficiency as a function of student, teacher, and school characteristics. It found that the average non-cognitive TEBC was 0.782, implying scope to increase non-cognitive outputs by about 22% while holding inputs constant, and that student disadvantage indicators (work, skipping whole days, and language barriers) significantly reduced non-cognitive efficiency. This indicates that improving learning environments and student wellbeing conditions—especially classroom climate and attendance-related supports—may raise both non-cognitive outcomes and overall school efficiency in LMIC, though associations cannot be interpreted causally.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA-D 2017 Grade 7+ (15-year-olds) — cognitive vs non-cognitive efficiency relationship
main_findings.target_variable: Correlation between cognitive and non-cognitive efficiency (country-specific association)
top_predictors: Country (Cambodia, Senegal, Zambia vs richer countries)
Student disadvantage indicators (language, work, health, truancy)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Whole-sample: positive association between cognitive and non-cognitive efficiency; country-specific correlations reported: Ecuador 0.111 (p=0.161), Guatemala 0.046 (p=0.545), Honduras 0.029 (p=0.691), Cambodia 0.161 (p=0.045), Paraguay −0.070 (p=0.356), Senegal 0.355 (p=0.000), Zambia 0.525 (p=0.000).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA-D 2017 Grade 7+ the study examined the relationship between cognitive and non-cognitive DEA efficiency scores across schools and found that the association is statistically significant and stronger in the poorest countries (Cambodia, Senegal, Zambia) but weaker or non-significant in richer countries. This indicates that efficiency-improving interventions in resource-constrained settings may simultaneously enhance both cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes, supporting integrated school improvement strategies, while still acknowledging that the evidence is correlational rather than causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA-D 2017 Grade 7+ (15-year-olds) — inequality vs efficiency trade-off
top_predictors: Proportion of low performers (Level 1 or below)
Inclusion (Level 2 or above prevalence among deprived students)
Correlation of achievement with family SES
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 4 (whole sample): Gini (math) −1.3898***; Gini (reading) −1.4123***; SD (math) 0.0015***; SD (reading) 0.0015***; Level 1 or below (math) −0.1276***; Level 1 or below (reading) −0.1427***. Table 4 also reports inclusion-related effects: Level 2 or above – low SES (math) −0.0101 (ns) and (reading) −0.0096 (ns); Level 2 or above – low education resource (math) 0.0619*** and (reading) 0.0151 (ns).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA-D 2017 Grade 7+ the study tested whether within-school inequality measures are associated with cognitive and non-cognitive efficiency and found no evidence of a trade-off: higher inequality (e.g., larger Gini and higher shares of Level 1 or below students) was associated with lower efficiency. This indicates that equity-oriented policies—such as reducing within-school achievement disparities and improving inclusion—can be pursued alongside efficiency goals in LMIC without sacrificing technical efficiency, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses the 2017 PISA for Development (PISA-D) learning survey at grade 7 (15-year-olds) or above in seven LMIC/economies (Cambodia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Senegal, Zambia). It merges student, teacher, and school/principal questionnaires and conducts a two-stage Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA): first estimating output-oriented technical efficiency frontiers for cognitive outcomes (math/reading/science using the first plausible value) and for non-cognitive outcomes (factor-derived indices of socialisation, attitudes, and feelings), then regressing bias-corrected efficiency scores on student, teacher, school, policy, and inequality indicators. Across 1180 schools, mean TEBC is 0.801 for cognitive and 0.782 for non-cognitive, implying potential efficiency gains of about 20–22% with inputs held constant. The paper reports bootstrap confidence intervals and marginal effects with bootstrapped standard errors, but it does not provide explicit survey-weight usage; results are therefore best interpreted as associations rather than causal effects, consistent with the cross-sectional nature of PISA-D.
